## Task 1: Reproducing and improving figures

```{r load-wrangle}
# load and wrangle the data here
data <- read_csv(here("data/HIIT-postpartum-depression.csv")) %>% 
  clean_names()
  
data[data == "#NULL!"] <- NA # standardising missing values to NA's instead of "#NULL!"
```


### Figure 3 - Kai
```{r figure-3}
# figure 3 data
figure3_data <- data %>%
  # assign readable interventions to groups
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      `intervention_group` == 1 ~ "HIIT – High Intensity Interval Training Group",
      `intervention_group` == 2 ~ "EDU – Educational Intervention Group"
    ),
    # create column for depression score cutoffs
    EPDS = as.numeric(`edinburg_postnatal_depression_scale_score`),
    category = case_when(
      EPDS < 10 ~ "range indicating the norm (below 10 points)",
      EPDS >= 10 & EPDS < 12 ~ "slightly increased severity of PPD symptoms (10-11 points)",
      EPDS >= 12 ~ "increased severity of PPD symptoms (12 or more points)"
    )
  ) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(number_of_hiit_sessions_own_activity)) %>% 
  # calculate percentages
  drop_na(category) %>%
  count(group, category) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n) * 100) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c(
      "HIIT – High Intensity Interval Training Group",
      "EDU – Educational Intervention Group"
    )),
    category = factor(category, levels = c( # assign factor levels to EPDS levels for correct visualisation
      "increased severity of PPD symptoms (12 or more points)",
      "slightly increased severity of PPD symptoms (10-11 points)",
      "range indicating the norm (below 10 points)"))
  )

# replicated figure 3
ggplot(figure3_data, aes(x = percent, y = group, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.4) +
  # x-axis percentage scale
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10),
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) +
  # bar colours
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "range indicating the norm (below 10 points)" = "#9EC1FF",
      "slightly increased severity of PPD symptoms (10-11 points)" = "#0B3C8A",
      "increased severity of PPD symptoms (12 or more points)" = "#C21F17"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  # remove axis names
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  # reverse EPDS levels in legend
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme(
    # general plot configuration
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 5, b = 90, l = 30),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.8),
    # legend configuration
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.spacing.y = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.width  = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.05, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
    legend.direction = "vertical",
    # axes configuration
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5, color = "black", hjust = 1, margin = margin(r = 1)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12, color = "black")
  )
```

```{r figure-3 improved}
# improved figure 3
ggplot(figure3_data, aes(x = percent, 
                         y = recode(group, # remove full name of interventions
                                    "HIIT – High Intensity Interval Training Group" = "HIIT",
                                    "EDU – Educational Intervention Group" = "EDU",), fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 10),
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) + # make percentage scale integer to reduce visual clutter
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c( # more communicative colours
      "range indicating the norm (below 10 points)" = "grey",
      "slightly increased severity of PPD symptoms (10-11 points)" = "skyblue",
      "increased severity of PPD symptoms (12 or more points)" = "dodgerblue"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "increased severity (>12 points)",
      "slightly increased severity (10-11 points)",
      "healthy (<10 points)" # name change to better represent severity level
    ),
    name = "Postpartum depression severity levels" # legend title for clarity
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", percent), "%")), # labels for bar proportions 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), 
            color = "black") +
  # add title and subtitle
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Distribution of Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Score (EDPS) by postpartum intervention",
    subtitle = "EDU = Educational Intervention, HIIT = High Intensity Interval Training"
  ) +
  # minimal theme to increase focus on the data
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1), # border to distinguish data from other info
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.direction = "vertical",
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

More progressive colours are used, with the distinct grey to communicate the healthy state as different from the two pathological ones. Added a title so the graph is self sufficient, and a subheading for acronyms so that they can be used on the y axis to give more space to the plot. Added percentage labels to the bars so the information being communicated is clearer, and minor breaks at each 5% interval for easier intuitive interpretation. Changed the label for severity under 10 points to a more accurate description.

### Figure 4 - James
```{r figure-4}
data_4 <- data %>%
  ## Convert Flourishing Scale scores from string into numeric values ##
  mutate(
    pre_fs_scale = as.numeric(pre_fs_scale),
    post_fs_score = as.numeric(post_fs_score),
    postnatal_florishing_scale_score = as.numeric(postnatal_florishing_scale_score)
    ) %>%
  ## Remove missing values, if not done, the calculated means will be wrong ##
  filter(
    !is.na(pre_fs_scale),
    !is.na(post_fs_score),
    !is.na(postnatal_florishing_scale_score)
    ) %>%
  ## Calculate means and standard deviations for each of the 3 time points ##
  group_by(intervention_group) %>%
  summarise(
    pre_mean = mean(pre_fs_scale),
    pre_sd = sd(pre_fs_scale),
    post_mean = mean(post_fs_score),
    post_sd = sd(post_fs_score),
    postnatal_mean = mean(postnatal_florishing_scale_score),
    postnatal_sd = sd(postnatal_florishing_scale_score)
    )

## Pivot the data so that the 3 time points can be plotted and labelled on the x-axis with standard deviations and means
data_4_long <- data_4 %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pre_mean, post_mean, postnatal_mean),
    names_to = "timepoint",
    values_to = "mean" # The pivot is only done to the means, the standard deviation can later be added manually.
    ) %>%
  mutate(
    sd = case_when(
      timepoint == "pre_mean" ~ pre_sd,
      timepoint == "post_mean" ~ post_sd,
      timepoint == "postnatal_mean" ~ postnatal_sd # Adds in the standard deviation for each time point manually
      ),
    timepoint = factor( 
      timepoint, 
      levels = c("pre_mean", "post_mean", "postnatal_mean"),
      labels = c("Before the intervention\n(II trimester of pregnancy)",
                 "After the intervention\n(III trimester of pregnancy)",
                 "Follow-up\n(± 5 months postpartum)" # Adds labels for each time point
                 )
      ),
    intervention_group = factor(intervention_group) # Makes intervention_group be treated as categorical
    )

## Plot the graph
ggplot(data_4_long, aes(x = timepoint, y = mean, group = intervention_group, linetype = factor(intervention_group))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.03, linetype = "solid") + # Creates error bars of the standard deviations
  ## 'M =' text on the graph is added ## 
  geom_text(aes(
    label = sprintf("M = %.2f", mean), # Adds 2 decimal points
    hjust = case_when(
    ## Shifts the first 2 'M = ' text labels to the left of the error bars, and the final one to the right
    grepl("Before|After", timepoint) ~ 1.2,
    grepl("Follow", timepoint) ~ -0.2
    ),
    ## Shifts the 'M = ' up and down as not to overlap with the line.
    vjust = case_when(
      grepl("Before", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, 1.3, 0.1), 
      grepl("After", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, -1.2, 1.8),
      grepl("Follow", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, 0.6, 0.6),
      )
    ),
    size = 3 # Set size of font
    ) +
  ## Legend configuration ##
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + # Moves legend to the bottom
  guides(linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) + # Stacks the legend guide for the lines
  scale_y_continuous(
    ## Y-axis configuration ##
    limits = c(40, 60), # Sets y-axis from 40 to 60 
    breaks = seq(40, 60, by = 2), # Adds ticks every 2 units
    labels = function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x) # Adds .00 to the y-axis
    ) +
  ## Line labelling ##
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("1" = "solid", "2" = "dotted"),
    labels = c("HIIT - High Intensity Interval Training Group", "EDU - Educational Intervention Group")
    ) + 
  ## Y-axis is labelled, however I have used the x label in order for it to be at the bottom. ##
  labs(
    x = "**Psychological well-being** (*measured with the Flourishing Scale*)",
    y = NULL,
    linetype = NULL
    ) +
  theme(
    axis.title.x = element_markdown(margin = margin(t = 15)), # Spaces the y-axis label to be more central
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Makes the legend icon for the lines' background transparent
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1), # Adds the black border around the graph
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA), # Makes background white
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey80", linetype), # Adds the major y-axis grid lines
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank() # Shouldn't be necessary, but I notice that there is a small vertical white line which interrupts the major y-axis grid lines without this.
    )
```

```{r figure-4 improved}
## Plot the graph
ggplot(data_4_long, aes(x = timepoint, y = mean, group = intervention_group, color = factor(intervention_group))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  # Creates error bars of the standard deviations
  ## 'M =' text on the graph is added ## 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.06, linetype = "solid", position = position_dodge(width = 0.03)) + # Error bars are shifted horizontally so no longer overlap
  geom_text(aes(
    label = sprintf("M = %.2f", mean), # Adds 2 decimal points to the 'M = '
    hjust = case_when(
    ## Shifts the first 2 'M = ' text labels to the left of the error bars, and the final one to the right
      grepl("Before|After", timepoint) ~ 1.2,
      grepl("Follow", timepoint) ~ -0.2
      ),
  vjust = case_when(
    ## Shifts the 'M = ' up and down as not to overlap with the line.
    grepl("Before", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, 1.3, 0.1),
    grepl("After", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, -1.2, 1.8),
    grepl("Follow", timepoint) ~ ifelse(intervention_group == 1, 0.6, 0.6)
    )
  ),
  size = 3.2, # Change size of 'M = ' text
  fontface = "bold", # Makes it bold
  show.legend = FALSE # Otherwise there will be an 'a' in the legend key overlapping with the line
  ) +
  ## Legend configuration ##
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + # Moves legend to the bottom
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) + # Stacks the legend guide for the lines
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(40, 56), # Sets y-axis from 40 to 60
    breaks = seq(40, 60, by = 2) # Sets ticks every 2 units
    ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("1" = "dodgerblue", "2" = "brown1"), # Sets contrasting colours for the lines
    labels = c("**HIIT** - High Intensity Interval Training Group", "**EDU** - Educational Intervention Group")
    ) + 
  ## Y-axis is labelled on y-axis, and legend is labelled.
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "**Psychological well-being** (*measured with the Flourishing Scale*)",
    color = "**Intervention Group** (*M = Mean*)"
    ) +
  theme(
    ## element_markdown() is used on several areas of the graph in order to make text bold using the ggtext package.
    axis.title.y = element_markdown(size = 10, margin = margin(t = 15, l = 10, r = 10)), # Y-axis is given margins to better fit onto graph.
    legend.title = element_markdown(),
    legend.text = element_markdown(),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Makes lines' key background transparent
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1), # Adds border around the graph
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA), # Makes graph background white
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey80"), # Adds major y-axis grid
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_line(color = "grey80"), # Adds minor y-axis grid
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank() # There is a small vertical white line which interrupts the major y-axis grid lines without this.
    )
```

Contrasting colours are used which makes the trend clear when one line overtakes the other, where before it was difficult to tell. Dotted line is now unnecessary and removed. Error bars shifted horizontally so no longer overlap. Decimals on y-axis removed, it’s just extra cluster. Moving y-axis label to y-axis for less cluster on bottom. Label for the legend with explanation for what M = means added. Added grid minor y so that error bars can be more accurately estimated. Made ‘M =’ bold so easily readable. Y-axis set to 56 to 40 so lines less compressed. Points are added for better visibility.

### Figure 5 - Fimi
```{r figure-5}
# original reproduction of figure 5
fig5 <- data %>% 
  # make a new column and make all the columns same value
  mutate(pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale = as.numeric(pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale),
         post_sf12_pcs = as.numeric(post_sf12_pcs),
         postnatal_sf_12_pcs = as.numeric(postnatal_sf_12_pcs),
         group = case_when(
           `intervention_group` == 1 ~ "HIIT – High Intensity Interval Training Group",
           `intervention_group` == 2 ~ "EDU – Educational Intervention Group")) %>%
  # filter out excluded participants
    filter(
    !is.na(pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale),
    !is.na(post_sf12_pcs),
    !is.na(postnatal_sf_12_pcs)
    ) %>%
  # select the groups physical health before, after and follow up from intervention
  select(participant_code, group, pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale, post_sf12_pcs,postnatal_sf_12_pcs) %>%
  
  # lengthens data and increase number of rows and decreases columns 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(
    pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale,
    post_sf12_pcs,
    postnatal_sf_12_pcs), 
    names_to = "time",
    values_to = "physical_health") %>% 
  
  # changes the name of the time columns to match intervention timing 
   mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c(
        "pre_sf_12_pcs_physicalhealthscale",
        "post_sf12_pcs",
        "postnatal_sf_12_pcs"),
      labels = c(
        "Before intervention 
        (II trimester of pregnancy)",
        "After intervention
        (III trimester of pregnancy)",
        "Follow-up
        (± 5 months postpartum"))) %>% 
    filter(!is.na(physical_health)) %>% 
    mutate(group = factor(group))
  
# Calculate mean and standard deviation
fig5_summary <- fig5 %>% 
  group_by(group, time) %>% 
  summarise(mean_physical = mean(physical_health, na.rm = TRUE), 
            sd_physical = sd(physical_health, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
 mutate(mean_round = round(mean_physical,2)) 


# plot replicated graph
ggplot(fig5_summary, aes(x=time,y=mean_physical,
                         group=group,
                         linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(size=0.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_physical-sd_physical,
    ymax = mean_physical+sd_physical
  ),
  width = 0.05) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("M =", mean_round)), 
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.2),
            vjust = -1,
            size = 3) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values=c("solid","dotted"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    x = bquote(bold("Physical health")~"(measured with the Short Form Health Survey-physical subscale)"),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) 
```

```{r}

group = intervention_group)) +
```

## Task 2: FAIR data principles
The data set is findable: with a unique and persistent DOI. There is metadata providing a description of the dataset along with a title, authors, date of publication, and the identifier of the dataset, on the dataset's page where it is indexed in the Mendeley Data repository. The data also does well in accessibility, as the DOI allows for direct access to the dataset using standard web protocol, there are no barriers to access and no closed system involved. The metadata would stay accessible if the data became no longer available because it is stored in a persistent page independent of the files. On interoperability, the dataset uses standardised international psychological and physical activity measurement tools like the Beck depression inventory II and Edinburgh postnatal depression scale, meaning the information can be understood well by health researchers. However, there is no reported use of ontological vocabularies with identifiers, so this is a point for possible improvement. The metadata does include explicit qualified references to other sources of information, clearly stating the relationship between the two data, such as the study the data comes from, the measurement tools used, and the trial registration ID. Lastly, to address reusability, the data and metadata are described thoroughly with reference made to study design, population, interventions and outcome measures. There is a visible creative commons data usage license on the repository page with explicit permissions for reuse of the data. The metadata clearly states the study that the data originates from with all relevant information about the study present as well. The metadata also meets the standards of health research, complying with CONSORT guidelines for information presentation and standardised measurements, while the repository page includes guidance on reproducing the research.(286 words)


## Task 3: Reproducibility brief
The strongest point for the study's reproducibility was its following of CONSORT reporting guidelines, ensuring transparency in relaying the results of the trial. It was also good practice to register a protocol for maintenance of the integrity of the study, which would inevitably have a positive impact on any repeat iteration of the methodology. The outcome measures used standardised and validated measurement tools like EPDS, BDI-II, Flourishing Scale, providing a well-reported method for determining outcomes, with clear cut offs and scoring. The statistical tests used were also well reported, with the software specified as SPSS v27, and a list of the exact tests used on display. The dataset for the results is also publicly available with a dedicated DOI and landing page in the Mendeley data repository, meaning anyone can carry out the analysis on the raw results. For points of improvement: there were no exact details about the HIIT group intervention, where there should have been information on interval structure, progression rules, exercise selection, decision rules for tailoring workouts etc. The results section of the study was also rather terse in relaying exact numbers, meaning this information has to be partially gleaned from just the visualisations. Some of the graphs are quite difficult to read, with compressed or overlapping parts in the figure, making interpretation of the results uncertain. When appraising the quality of a reproduced study, the matching of the new results to the original is paramount so this is a sizeable obstacle in that regard. The study design itself makes external reproducibility rather difficult as the sample population is exclusively Caucasian Polish, and engages with only one healthcare system, thus the results will likely be different in a sample without this narrow demographic profile. (287 words)
